pages.text: Put a full bottle of water in a freezer overnight. In the morning the bottle is swollen, and if it was glass it may have cracked. A sachet of water frozen solid is tight and round like a small pillow. Drop a lump of that ice into a cup of sobolo and it floats. We see these things so often that we forget to ask why. Yet they are strange. Almost every other substance shrinks when it freezes, and its solid form sinks in its liquid. Water breaks the rule, and life on Earth depends on it.

pages.text: Start with the rule. All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving. Heat a substance and its particles move faster and push further apart, so it takes up more space. This is expansion. Cool it and the particles slow down and draw closer, so it shrinks. This is contraction. You can see both around you. Electricity wires hang lower on a hot afternoon than at dawn. Builders leave small gaps between the sections of a bridge, so that the sections can expand in the heat without cracking. A metal roof creaks as it warms in the morning and cools in the evening.

Cool it and the particles slow down and draw closer, so it shrinks.
This is contraction.
You can see both around you.
Electricity wires hang lower on a hot afternoon than at dawn.
Builders leave small gaps between the sections of a bridge, so that the sections can expand in the heat without cracking.
A metal roof creaks as it warms in the morning and cools in the evening.
pages.alt: Electricity wires sagging between poles in the afternoon sun, and a narrow gap between two sections of a bridge.

pages.text: When a substance contracts, the same mass is packed into less space. We say that its density has increased. Density tells us how much mass is in each unit of volume: density = mass ÷ volume. Water has a density of 1 gram per cubic centimetre. An object that is less dense than a liquid floats in it, and one that is denser sinks. Palm oil floats on water. A stone sinks. Since most substances contract as they cool and freeze, their solids are denser than their liquids. Drop a piece of solid candle wax into melted wax and it goes to the bottom.

pages.text: Water follows the rule until it is cooled to 4 °C. At that temperature it is at its densest. Cool it further and it does something unexpected: it begins to expand. At 0 °C it freezes, and its particles lock together in an open pattern with more empty space between them than in the liquid. Ice therefore takes up about 9 per cent more room than the water it was made from, and its density is only about 0.92 grams per cubic centimetre. That is why the bottle swells, why the sachet tightens, and why ice floats with only a small part of it above the surface.

pages.text: This odd behaviour protects life in cold countries. In winter, the water at the surface of a lake cools, becomes denser, and sinks, until the whole lake is at 4 °C. After that, colder water is lighter, so it stays on top and freezes there. The sheet of ice floats and acts as a blanket, keeping the water below it liquid. Fish and other living things survive under it until spring. If ice were denser than water, it would sink. Lakes would freeze from the bottom up into solid blocks, and little could live in them.

Fish and other living things survive under it until spring.

Lakes would freeze from the bottom up into solid blocks, and little could live in them.
pages.alt: A cross-section of a frozen lake with a layer of ice on top and fish swimming in the liquid water beneath.

pages.text: Expanding ice is also a powerful tool. Water seeps into cracks in rock, freezes, expands, and forces the cracks wider. Over many years this breaks mountains into soil. In cold countries, it bursts water pipes and breaks up roads. At sea, huge icebergs float with about nine-tenths of their ice hidden under the water, a danger to ships. Ghana has no frozen lakes, but the same science is in every kitchen. Leave space at the top of a bottle before you freeze it. And never put a sealed glass bottle in the freezer: the water will expand, and glass cannot stretch.

Apply it: A trader wants to freeze bottles of water to sell. What should she do, and why?
options: Fill each bottle to the very top, because ice shrinks
Leave some space in each bottle, because water expands as it freezes
Use sealed glass bottles, because glass stretches

activities.prompt: Put the steps in order to show how a lake freezes in a cold country.
items: Cold air cools the water at the surface
The cooled water becomes denser and sinks
Water colder than 4 °C stays on top and freezes
A floating sheet of ice keeps the water below liquid
